title: Winter Storm Elliott Recommendation #11: EIPC Study

sentences.text: MRO Midwest Reliability Organization NPCC Northeast Power Coordinating Council RF ReliabilityFirst SERC SERC Reliability Corporation Texas RE Texas Reliability Entity WECC Western Electric Coordinating Council Executive Summary FERC NERC Joint Report From December 21 through 26, 2022, Winter Storm Elliott produced extreme cold weather that caused generation outages and unavailability that threatened the reliability of the BES.

In response, FERC and NERC jointly authored the report, Inquiry into Bulk-Power System Operations During December 2022 Winter Storm Elliott 1, which explained major causes for the generation outages and made recommendations to the industry for how to prevent such outages in the future.
The comparative analysis showed that during Winter Storm Elliott, system inertia was robust and the risk of underfrequency load shedding (UFLS) in the Eastern Interconnection (EI) was low.
The consensus from this analysis is that Winter Storm Elliott was a resource adequacy event and not a low inertia risk.

1 Inquiry into Bulk-Power System Operations During December 2022 Winter Storm Elliott 2https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5b1032e545776e01e7058845/t/65cfa63c13bfb16c3c4ec4aa/1708107325559/EIPC+FRWG+2022+Final+Report+-+2- 10-24.pdf Chapter 1: Data Collection Data Collection According to the 1-minute average data provided by NERC and represented in Figure 1.1 of the joint report, the lowest frequency observed during Winter Storm Elliott was 59.936 Hz on December 24 at 4:24 AM.
Based upon this data from EIDSN, the EI system inertia, total load, and rate of change of frequency (ROCOF) do not appear unusual during Winter Storm Elliott (see Figure 1.2).

In Scenario 2, online system inertia is 1,069 GW-s, and the analysis tested a 10 GW source loss.
The study showed that the EI frequency would dip to 59.65 Hz, which is above the EI UFLS threshold of 59.6Hz.
As noted above, the lowest frequency recorded was 59.936 Hz – 0.286 Hz higher than in Scenario 2 and 0.336 Hz above the EI UFLS threshold.
As you can see, both system load and system inertia were at their highest on December 24, 2022, the date on which the lowest frequency occurred.

Figure 2.1: Average Load (GW) and Average Inertia (GW-s) Chapter 3: Comparison to Other Events Comparisons to Winter Storm Uri Winter Storm Uri was a severe cold-weather event that occurred between February 8, 2021 and February 20, 2021.
In ERCOT, demand-side load resources start disconnecting when frequency goes below 59.7Hz.
If frequency continues to drop, UFLS triggers at 59.3Hz.
During Winter Storm Uri, roughly 276 MW of load tripped due to UFLS as the frequency barely touched 59.3 Hz, despite the controlled firm load shed.
The system load was at a record high of 69,871 MW.
Due to the difference in sizes of the two interconnections, EI’s total system inertia is much higher and results in lower frequency decline and lower ROCOF.
According to EIPC analysis, the EI is not at a risk of reaching UFLS trigger for frequency events for the expected resource mix in the next 5 years.

Chapter 3: Comparison to Other Events Notable Generation Trip Events The following FNET data shows three of the largest generation trip events during Winter Storm Elliott (Table 3.1, Table 3.2, and Table 3.3).
The largest (based on the available data) was 880 MW, after which EI frequency declined from 59.986 Hz to 59.95 Hz Table 3.3).
This is the typical frequency decline for such an event.
In practice, several stabilizing mechanisms-including governor responses, load sensitivity, etc. activate within seconds to significantly mitigate the rate of frequency decline.

Chapter 4: Conclusion Based on the system inertia available during the worst conditions of Winter Storm Elliott compared to the scenarios studied by the EIPC FRWG, we conclude that UFLS would not have been triggered in the EI even for a loss of 10,000 MW during Winter Storm Elliott.
The comparative analysis showed that during Winter Storm Elliott, system inertia was robust and the risk of underfrequency load shedding (UFLS) in the Eastern Interconnection (EI) was low.
Further analysis of generation trips and frequency oscillation on the system showed that the system maintained dynamic stability.
